issues.legal_issue: The exclusion of residential tenants from rent-control protection above a rent threshold, while tenants of non-residential buildings remain protected regardless of rent, lacks a reasonable basis and violates equal protection.
material_facts: The rent-control law generally regulated tenancy, controlled rents, and prevented unreasonable eviction for residential and non-residential buildings.
The challenged provision excluded residential buildings or parts occupied by a tenant paying rent above the prescribed threshold from the law’s protections.
The rent-based exception for non-residential buildings had been removed, so tenants of those buildings remained protected regardless of the rent they paid.

The State did not show that residential tenants were less in need of protection than non-residential tenants, or that excluding higher-rent residential tenants would protect weaker sections of society.
The threshold had been set years earlier, and the Court took judicial notice that rents had increased substantially, making the threshold artificial and irrelevant in practice.
issues.conclusion: The Court struck down the residential rent-based exemption as unconstitutional because it violated Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification only when it rests on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the law’s objective. The Court found no reasonable nexus between the distinction based on building use and rent and the Act’s objectives of regulating tenancies, controlling rents, and preventing unreasonable eviction. A provision that was valid when enacted may become discriminatory and unconstitutional as circumstances change; the Court relied on Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh, [1984] 1 SCC 222, for that principle. It distinguished Raval & Co. v. Ramachandran, [1974] 2 SCR 629, because the observations there were made in a different context and not on a challenge under Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_based_t: A constitutional challenge is brought against an exemption from tenant-protection rules based on rent.
predicates.residential_tenants_above_rent_threshold: Residential tenants paying rent above a threshold are excluded from the protections available to other tenants.
predicates.nonresidential_tenants_remain_protected_: Tenants of non-residential buildings remain protected regardless of the rent they pay.
predicates.state_did_not_show_residential_tenants_n: The government did not establish that residential tenants need less protection than tenants of non-residential buildings.
predicates.rent_threshold_became_unrealistic: Substantial rent increases made the threshold unrealistic in relation to prevailing rents.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a rent-based tenant-protection exemption, residential tenants above the threshold are excluded, non-residential tenants remain protected regardless of rent, the government has not shown residential tenants need less protection, and the threshold has become unrealistic, the exemption is unconstitutional.
